title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up. 
            
                        
                
                    
                                            
                
                
                                            
    More by Emily

body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

title: We Now Know When Apple's Big iPhone Event Will Happen
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 26, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Viva Tung/Lifehacker
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just announced a new keynote, where the company is expected to announce the latest iPhones.
                                            Leaks and rumors suggest Apple will reveal the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which should offer small upgrades over the iPhone 17 Pro.
                                            The star of the show will be the iPhone Ultra, Apple's first foldable iPhone (and likely the company's most expensive iPhone to date).
                                            The keynote starts at 10 a.m. PT on Wednesday, Sept. 9.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You don't need to follow leaks and rumors to know that Apple will announce the iPhone 18 next month. The company has revealed new iPhones once a year every year since its first smartphone launch back in 2007. The real unknown, of course, is what day exactly Apple will make these announcements. As of Wednesday, we know for sure. Ahead of the event, make sure to enter Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game. The quiz is now in its third round, and each correct guess gets you the chance to win the latest Apple Watch.Apple just announced its next big iPhone eventApple has set an official time and date for its iPhone 18 announcement. The company is scheduled to kick off its keynote on Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 10 a.m. PT. While Apple is inviting some media members to attend in person, anyone can watch the presentation live online. Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, confirmed the keynote in a post on X:

    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    

What will Apple announce at its iPhone event?We don't know for sure what Apple will reveal on Sept. 9, but leaks and rumors give us some good guesses. The math tells us that Apple will go from the iPhone 17 to the iPhone 18 this year, while the leaks suggest that we'll see the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the foldable "iPhone Ultra."(Apple may delay the standard iPhone 18 to 2027, per rumors.) 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will likely be standard upgrades from the iPhone 17 Pro series: Expect better cameras, bigger batteries, new colors (including the new "light blue" and "dark cherry"), the new A20 chip, and higher price tags. The star of the show will be Apple's first foldable iPhone, which will come with many of the same internals as the iPhone 18 Pros, but may ship with Touch ID instead of Face ID, and, of course, with two display types: a smaller outer display, which opens up to reveal a larger inner display. This might be Apple's most expensive iPhone yet, fetching over $2,000, but we'll have to wait and see once Apple officially announces its price tag.

                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.

title: This Is the Best Ad-Free Alternative to Apple Maps
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 26, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Prykhodov via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple Maps officially launched ads in search this week.
                                            You'll see ads in the new "Suggested Places" field, as well as in Apple Maps search results.
                                            You can't block Apple Maps ads, but you can choose an alternative that skips out on them completely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        This week, Apple Maps officially launched ads in search. It's not necessarily a surprise, mind you: We learned back in October that Apple planned to roll out ads at some point. But it's still a bit jarring to see Apple actually commit to the plan. Now, most of the mainstream navigation apps come with ads, which makes getting around without dealing with ads difficult—but not impossible.How Apple Maps' ads work Once ads hit your app, you'll start seeing them when you search for new destinations. That includes both in the new "Suggested Places" section, as well as within search results as well. Like other platforms that float sponsored items to the top of search results, you'll likely want to be a bit more scrupulous, since the top pick might not actually be the most relevant to your query. What's more, there's no way to actually disable these ads. There are ad blockers for iPhone, but they're limited, and won't block Apple's own ads. As such, it just doesn't feel very "Apple" to deal with ads on the company's own navigation app—especially if you're already giving Apple money every month. While Apple Maps doesn't have a paid subscription, Apple offers plenty of services at a cost. As YouTuber Quinn Nelson notes, some users are paying $50 per month for Apple One, and still having to deal with ads on Apple Maps. Of course, it's the same story for Google Maps: Google's famous navigation app also has mandatory ads, whether you subscribe to one of Google's services or not. In Apple's view, its approach is better than competitors like Google, as the company is adamant its ads preserve your privacy. But even if that's the case, I'm not sure it's going to sell users on the new approach.
It's tough to find a good navigation alternative to Apple Maps or Google Maps. That includes Waze, which is also owned by Google and also has ads. However, there is one solid—albeit rather underground—choice for anyone whose top priority is a lack of ads.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Organic Maps is a free and open-source app that prioritizes privacy for navigation. According to the developer, the app works entirely offline, and does not track people as they use it. (How refreshing.) As such, you could download your maps, disable cellular services, and still have the ability to navigate—of course, you can use it while connected, as well. The app supports a number of features that you'll find on other more mainstream platforms, including cycling and hiking routes, turn-by-turn directions, public transit maps, and dark mode. Organic Maps uses OpenStreetMap to provide its navigation data. While the benefit of OpenStreetMap is that it's also open-source, so users all over the globe can add their own data points, it likely isn't as robust as Apple's map data, not to mention Google's decades of data. Still, users have generally positive reviews on the iOS App Store, suggesting that OpenStreetMap's data offers an adequate alternative to Apple Maps. Now, if you're used to scrolling through restaurant reviews or checking out Street View, you'll miss that here. While Organic Maps does have a search function, it's lacking compared to other platforms. This is definitely a navigation-first app, rather than a full Apple Maps or Google Maps replacement. Still, if you're looking for an ad-free alternative, there are few better options out there at this time.

schema.headline: This Is the Best Ad-Free Alternative to Apple Maps

            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            TikTok announced four new features coming to its comment section over the next month.
                                            Next month, the app will roll out voice comments, which will let users record and post audio up to 60 seconds.
                                            Creators can add polls to their comment sections to invite viewers to vote on up to five options at a time.
                                            Finally, TikTok is rolling out photo carousel and Live Photos comments as well.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TikTok is famous for its addictive algorithm. And while the videos are certainly the app's main focus, I find the most entertainment in the comments. TikTok commenters can be hilarious, especially since they can use both text and photos to make their jokes. Social media comments are often vile, and while TikTok isn't immune to trolls and their ilk, its comments are generally something else. Now, the comments are changing. On Thursday, TikTok announced four new features that will make comments more visual, interactive, and, well, loud. Not all of these features are out quite yet, but by next month, you might not recognize TikTok's comment section. Text and photo comments aren't going anywhere, but you may find that the comment section is about to get a bit louder. Starting next month, TikTok will support voice comments up to 60 seconds long, which adds a wholly unique type of comment to the mix. Based on TikTok's press release, you can still attach a text-based comment to your voice comment, similar to how photo comments work.While friends may post voice comments on each other's videos à la voice memos in a group chat, I'm guessing that commenters in general will use this feature in ways TikTok doesn't necessarily intend. In fact, this may birth a new type of meme, where users spam videos with obnoxious sound effects and reaction sounds. Think the sounds added to meme edits of viral videos, but in comment form. It's going to be messy, and, likely, hysterical.   
Starting this week, you may see a new interactive element to TikTok comments: polls. TikTok says creators can add polls to the comments of their videos, with up to five voting options per poll. Rather than ask for opinions in the comments, creators can use a poll instead. Creators can choose how long voting lasts, and watch votes appear in real time. It's a small change, but one that could be useful to both big and small creators looking for input from their viewers. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You're no longer limited to posting static images in TikTok's comments. TikTok now supports uploading Live Photos to comments, which should also prove interesting. I could see people thinking they're posting a standard image, but accidentally uploading a Live Photo instead. But seeing as users already know how to add GIFs to comments, I'm not sure how many will want to upload Live Photos. This one might be reserved more for friends commenting on friends' videos, but we'll have to see how users react to know for sure. This last update is perhaps a bit more useful than Live Photo comments. TikTok says it's working on allowing users to upload up to nine photos in one comment, which means the comments section may be literally full of pictures once this launches en masse.  Like standard carousels, users will be able to swipe through your photo uploads, including in a full-screen view. This one will roll out over the course of this month.

title: I Let ChatGPT Sign Into My Web Accounts for Me, and It Was More Trouble Than It’s Worth
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 3, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT Work can now sign into websites on your behalf.
                                            You can enter credentials manually or via a password manager.
                                            Once given access, the AI can complete tasks in your accounts.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        AI agents are becoming more capable over time, and the latest ability rolled out to ChatGPT Work (that's the agentic bit of ChatGPT) is being able to sign into websites—and in theory, taking even more of your workload off you. The official examples of how you might want to use this include setting up utilities for a new apartment, organizing an appointment with a doctor, and canceling tickets for a rescheduled trip. "If it's something you’d normally have to open a browser and click through yourself, try asking ChatGPT Work to do it," says the sales pitch.I'm all for saving time on admin, but handing over my login credentials to ChatGPT feels like a bold step. Can I trust ChatGPT to keep my details safe and secure? And what are the chances of it going haywire once it's in my accounts? In the interests of finding out, I let it log into some of my less important accounts to see what it could do.This feature is rolling out now in the web and mobile apps for those on ChatGPT Plus, Pro, and Business accounts.
Will ChatGPT store your usernames and passwords?According to the ChatGPT release notes for August 25, 2026, "ChatGPT cannot see your username or password, and they are never seen by the model or used in model training. ChatGPT does not store your username or passwords." So how does it work if your usernames or passwords are never stored? The most basic option here is to simply sign in through ChatGPT when prompted by a site or app (and clear any two-factor authentication challenges at the same time), and then have the AI stay logged in for future tasks.The more advanced version, which is where you save a more significant chunk of time, is to give ChatGPT permission to interface with a third-party password manager. ChatGPT doesn't specify a list of supported password managers, but as far as I can tell, this is just for mobile: Any password manager on your phone can pop up when ChatGPT needs it and supply the relevant credentials.
    
            
            Browser data can be managed inside ChatGPT.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Underpinning all this is an actual browser, built into ChatGPT, that it can access and operate itself. Your accounts will see it as a new sign in (like they would if you signed in from a new device), and some websites and apps will let you mark ChatGPT as a "trusted" operator that can log in again in the future,You can control the data held by this browser: From ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Cloud browser. You can delete stored cookies from here, for example, which will effectively kick the AI out of any sites it has access to. As per ChatGPT support: "You stay in control of which websites ChatGPT Work can access, and it will always ask for confirmation before consequential actions, such as completing a reservation or payment." Exactly how it can tell when it's about to do something consequential, however, isn't clear.Here's what happened when I gave ChatGPT some tasks to do for meIf you want to make use of this inside ChatGPT on the web, click Work at the top of the screen to switch to agent mode, then tell the AI what you want to do: Something like "sign into my eBay account and tell me how my auctions are doing" or "sign into my accounting app and submit these invoices."I gave the eBay one a go first—the process proved to be incredibly slow for whatever reason, and I could've signed in multiple times in the normal way by the time ChatGPT got around to gaining access. There are also problems where the ChatGPT conversation tends to obfuscate what's going on: It asked for a verification code, and I didn't know where to check for it.You can, at any point, switch to the ChatGPT browser itself, which I eventually did to get through the verification code stage (it was sent over text). The AI was then able to correctly tell me what the current auction prices were on the items I was bidding on, after initially stumbling through several wrong pages—there's a thumbnail of the live browser in the corner of the screen, so you can see what's happening.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
            
            The built-in web browser can be opened or hidden.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Next up, I tasked ChatGPT with getting into my Airbnb account and finding some great spots close to Santa Cruz, Calif., within a certain price range. Again, I had to switch to the actual browser view to sign in (I was told the Airbnb site wasn't cooperating), but once I had given the AI access, it worked smoothly enough, looking up properties and giving me a rundown of prices.At the moment, the sign-in flows are just too finicky. Sites seem suspicious of the AI browser, everything is really slow, and you run into complications with verification codes, passkeys, and the like. You'll often have to manually sign in as you would anyway in order to get ChatGPT up and running on a site.
    
            
            ChatGPT can retrieve information okay, but tends to take its time.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Once that's done, though, everything works reasonably impressively, as long as you're giving commands that are fairly easy to interpret and carry out. ChatGPT on Airbnb seems competent with dates and locations, but I'm not sure it could filter through places based on the view or the general vibe of the decor.Perhaps most importantly, I still don't trust the AI to do these jobs better than I can, even if it can (eventually) do it more quickly. I want to see for myself what an Airbnb looks like, or who's bidding on an eBay auction, or what the available time slots are for an appointment to get my car serviced—if I left it to ChatGPT, I'd be too worried about it missing something (I have the same reservations about letting friends and family do things for me as well, but that's another issue).In my testing, ChatGPT didn't fail in any of the tasks I gave it once it had gained access to these sites, or give me any inaccurate answers, but that would always be at the back of my mind if I switched over to this completely. For now, I'm going to stick to these online admin tasks myself.

title: Apple Changed Its Mind on That Awful 'Hide My Email' Update
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 25, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: stockcam/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is no longer planning to make it more evident whenever you are using a Hide My Email alias.
                                            As designed, Hide My Email aliases use the same @icloud.com domain as typical iCloud email addresses.
                                            The new policy would use the @private.icloud.com domain, which would make it obvious when using an alias.
                                            Luckily, Apple is now officially reversing course, and continuing with the iCloud.com domain as usual.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I use Apple's "Hide My Email" feature virtually every time an app asks me for an email address. I almost never share my actual email, unless I really trust the company or service asking for it or know it'll make my life easier in the long run. (If you've ever tried confirming a Hide My Email alias with a customer service rep, you know what I mean.) If you're like me, you might have noticed some headlines earlier this summer about Apple's plans to reduce Hide My Email's efficacy. This was true, and, as designed, Apple's changes would have made it more likely that users would share their real email addresses whenever they signed up for services. But luckily, Apple is now cancelling those plans. What is Hide My Email?If you aren't familiar with this privacy tool, here's the gist: If you have an iCloud+ subscription, Hide My Email generates email "aliases" that forward messages to your real email address. You can use these aliases anywhere you would normally use your actual email, retaining some anonymity without sacrificing the convenience of using a single inbox. 
Let's say you're signing up for a new account somewhere. Rather than use your real email address when asked, you can use Hide My Email to generate a unique, random address—something like "[email protected]" (seriously, they really look like this). As silly as the aliases can be, they're invaluable for preserving your privacy: Any messages sent to these aliases will forward to your actual inbox. You'll receive the email as if someone sent it to your real address, without ever actually exposing your address to the contact. What's more, if that alias is ever compromised, you can shut it down without affecting your actual email address. Win-win. How Apple planned to make Hide My Email worseThis system has been working for years without issue. So, naturally, Apple planned on making things worse. Back in June, we learned the company had prepped to unify its "Hide My Email" alias domains with "Sign in with Apple" domains. If you've ever used Sign in with Apple—the feature that lets you sign up for services with your Apple Account—you may know the feature generates privaterelay.appleid.com domains for your account address. Per Apple, both Sign in with Apple and Hide My Email would use private.icloud.com domains. In the example above, your email alias would be "[email protected]" instead of "[email protected]."From Apple's perspective, this would simplify its processes, keeping both of its privacy login features tied to the same domain. But for the rest of us, it would break Hide My Email a bit. The original design ensures that your Hide My Email alias cannot be distinguished from a standard iCloud email. While a human might see [email protected] and know something's odd, a system will only know that the email address is a valid @icloud.com address. As such, it treats the alias as any other iCloud email, and lets you through. The new domain, however, signals to anyone (or any system) that your email address is actually an alias. Companies could potentially block @private.icloud.com domains from signing up for services, defeating the purpose of Hide My Email entirely. Apple had said existing Hide My Email domains would continue to operate normally, so your old aliases would carry on fine. But once the planned changes were supposed to take effect, new aliases would run the risk of failure. I would begrudgingly continue using the feature if most companies and services didn't end up treating @private.icloud.com addresses any differently from a typical domain. But if it becomes commonplace to block these Hide My Email aliases, that would change things.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Hide My Email will continue to work as designedFortunately, we don't need to worry about this anymore. On Monday, Apple issued an update, informing users that Hide My Email will remain on the iCloud.com domain. The update was brief, but Apple did say that the reversal came after "further consideration and reviewing community feedback," suggesting that the public outcry had an impact on this decision. Unfortunately for Apple, this wasn't the only Hide My Email controversy to land this summer. In July, we learned that Hide My Email had a security flaw that could leak your actual email address to bad actors—defeating the purpose of the feature entirely. A security researcher reported the flaw to Apple back in June of 2025, and while the company said it was working to fix it, the flaw persisted through this year. 404 Media initially broke the story, and, about three weeks later, Apple implemented a fix. As it stands, the feature should be secure, and should now continue to work as usual, but it's been a tough summer for Hide My Email.  Email alias alternatives you can use insteadIt isn't an issue now that Hide My Email isn't changing, but if you've decided you've had it with Apple, there are email alias alternatives out there you can try. Proton Mail, for example, has its own version of the feature, and while it requires a paid subscription for unlimited aliases, you can generate 10 for free. DuckDuckGo has its own version too, called Email Protection, which generates aliases using the domain @duck.com. Mozilla has an option in Firefox Relay, which also works with phone numbers.

title: Here's How to Protect Your Privacy If Someone Is Recording You With Their Glasses

body:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
        
        Meta’s smart glasses are earning a reputation for being a privacy nightmare—to put it mildly. While the company is taking steps to make it harder to record people without their knowledge, it’s still not possible to prevent being recorded. So, what can you do if you think someone is using their glasses to record you without your consent?
Know your rights if someone is recording youKnowing whether or not someone is legally allowed to record you won’t necessarily protect you from being recorded, but it’s a solid foundation to start with. And determining whether someone can record you generally boils down to two basic questions: Do you have a reasonable expectation of privacy? And do you live in a one- or two-party consent state?In the United States, a reasonable expectation of privacy is a legal principle that can help determine whether you have a right not to be recorded (in other jurisdictions, this concept may have a different name or criteria). The classic example of this would be standing outside on the street, but pointing a camera inside a person’s window. Even though the person recording outside is technically “in public,” the subject being recorded has a reasonable expectation that being inside their home entitles them to privacy—yes, even if the window is open.
When it comes to smart glasses, this principle applies as it would with any other camera. If someone tries to record you in a place where you have a reasonable expectation of privacy—your home, hotel room, or a bathroom, for example—then they are legally in the wrong.Within places that have a reasonable expectation of privacy, some places in the U.S. require that both parties to a conversation consent to it being recorded, while others require only one party to consent. The key here is that in all cases, the person recording must be a participant in the conversation. A third party listening in by pointing a camera or a microphone at you never has a right to record you in a place where you can reasonably expect privacy.This also means that even if the person wearing smart glasses is part of the conversation, recording you still might be illegal if you’re in a two-party consent state. Obviously, none of this applies when you’re in public places, or even on private property that’s open to the public like a restaurant or store, but it’s usually worth knowing your rights.Just because you have a legal right to privacy doesn’t mean you can prevent someone from recording you, but it can put you in a better position to have footage of you taken down or taking legal action against it in the future. And if you control the space where someone is recording you—say, inside your own home—you can always have them removed.Appeal to private authoritiesYour legal rights only matter so much in the moment if you’re faced with someone who won’t take no for an answer. Take this incident earlier this year, where a man filmed himself accosting British comedian Diane Morgan in the middle of a shoot. While the film crew in this instance obviously didn’t have a legal right to privacy, and probably did not have a legal right to remove the intruder, the person filming also clearly wasn’t deterred by potentially incurring a harassment charge. So, what can you do if someone simply won’t relent?In public-accessible spaces, your best bet is likely to find whoever owns or manages the space you’re in. You might not have the ability to stop someone from recording you inside a Starbucks, but the manager can kick them out if they’re causing a problem. Some places and organizations have started banning the use of recording-capable glasses altogether—so it's worth familiarizing yourself with the policies of the local businesses where you hang out. If you think someone’s recording you in public, it can be helpful to know if there’s a local bar or bookstore that bans these glasses. Even if it’s just to have a place to duck into if someone is recording you nearby, or to know who to ask for help to get someone to stop bothering you.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
More tips to prevent being recordedGetting someone to stop recording or observing you entirely is the ideal, but if that’s not an option, you might have to resort to some more creative solutions. Including, but not limited to the following:Try the Nearby Glasses app. This open-source application is available for Android and iOS, and can potentially identify nearby smart glasses. It uses Bluetooth data from nearby devices to try to determine if any smart glasses are in your vicinity. It’s not 100% reliable, but it can be a helpful indicator. It should also go without saying, but knowing that someone nearby has smart glasses doesn’t mean you know who is wearing them. So be careful before approaching someone that you’re not sure is wearing them.Watch for signs of tampering on the notification LED. Meta’s smart glasses are supposed to have an LED that alerts people around the user that a recording is in progress. A recent update is supposed to ensure that recording will cease if the LED is covered, but it’s still possible to tamper with the glasses to prevent this. It’s not great if someone is recording you without your permission, but if you see someone who appears to have visibly modified their smart glasses to prevent people from noticing the recording, then it’s extra important to take action.Don’t bother playing Disney music. One common tip you’ll find is to play copyrighted music from a particularly litigious company. The idea here is that, if the offending recorder tries to upload the footage to a site like YouTube or TikTok, then it could potentially get removed on copyright grounds.This isn’t really how those platforms often work. Content can get taken down due to a copyright claim, but just as often it can either get demonetized or simply muted. And in those cases, the copyright system isn’t really going to help you. Playing music to drown out a conversation might not hurt, but it’s better to rely on your own privacy complaints to take down videos, rather than hoping Disney will save you.

                What do you think so far?
